articles.title: In 1949, Pennsylvania shoe salesman Mahlon Haines built a 25-foot-tall work-boot house for $26,000; after falling into ruin, his granddaughter restored it and guests can now sleep inside
articles.summary: US News: What began as an audacious advertising idea for a Pennsylvania shoe businessman in the 1940s is now a roadside landmark where visitors can actually sp.
articles.body: What began as an audacious advertising idea for a Pennsylvania shoe businessman in the 1940s is now a roadside landmark where visitors can actually spend the night. The Haines Shoe House, a 25-foot-tall building shaped like a work boot, was built by shoe entrepreneur Mahlon Haines and today operates as a short-term rental. According to the Haines Shoe House’s official history, construction began in 1948 and the first guests arrived in 1949. The building cost $26,000 at the time. The Library of Congress also dates its construction to 1948-49. Located in Hellam Township, near York, the unusual structure measures about 48 feet long, 17 feet wide and 25 feet high. Its design was deliberately shaped like a high-topped work shoe, making it an early example of what architects describe as programmatic architecture, buildings designed to resemble or directly represent the purpose, product or idea they are associated with.A shoe salesman turned advertising into architectureHaines, known locally as the “Shoe Wizard”, built the house as a promotional attraction for his shoe business. Rather than simply putting up another sign, he created a building that could hardly be missed by people travelling through the area.The shoe theme extends beyond its exterior. Inside, the rooms are arranged within different parts of the boot, with the living room occupying the toe, the kitchen in the heel, bedrooms in the ankle and a recreation area in the instep. The building also features shoe-themed details, including stained glass. But Haines did not build the enormous shoe as his own home.From honeymoon getaway to ice-cream parlourThe Shoe House was originally used as a guest house. Haines made it available to elderly couples celebrating anniversaries and, for a period, honeymooning couples connected to towns where his stores operated. After Haines died in 1962, the property passed to his employees, who sold it in 1964. It subsequently spent years as a tourist attraction and ice-cream parlour, drawing visitors curious to see what a life-sized shoe looked like from the inside. Over time, however, the landmark fell into disrepair.His granddaughter brought the Shoe House backIn 1987, Haines’ granddaughter, Annie Haines Keller, bought the deteriorating property and began restoring it. The restoration brought the Shoe House back into use as a historic attraction and helped preserve an unusual piece of Pennsylvania’s roadside history.The property changed hands several more times over the following decades, with successive owners carrying out repairs and preservation work. In 2022, it was sold to Waylon and Naomi Brown, who gave the building further improvements and converted its use into a short-term rental.You can now sleep inside the giant bootThe Shoe House is no longer open for ordinary public tours. Instead, registered guests can rent the entire property for groups of up to six people. The roughly 1,500-square-foot building has three bedrooms, two-and-a-half bathrooms, a living room, kitchen/dinette and recreation room spread across its unusual five levels. Narrow staircases connect the spaces, adding another reminder that this is less a conventional house than a piece of architectural theatre.The landmark also received a Pennsylvania state historical marker in 2023, formally recognising its place in the state’s history. More than seven decades after Mahlon Haines turned a work boot into an advertising spectacle, the idea still works. The building remains impossible to mistake for anything else, and, for those who book a stay, the giant shoe is no longer just something to photograph from the road. It is a place to sleep.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: El Niño just leveled up to super status. Here’s what that means for the weather
articles.summary: An already-strong El Niño just turned super as the phenomenon crosses into unprecedented territory.
articles.body: An already-strong El Niño just turned super as the phenomenon crosses into unprecedented territory. The natural climate cycle has been strengthening at a breakneck pace since it was first declared in June and is stronger now than it’s ever been on this date. And isn’t done bulking up yet. ☀️ Get your local forecast from the CNN Weather app Forecasters have thought for months that El Niño would become very strong or “super” by this fall. The key measure of its strength has now crossed that threshold and will continue to soar higher. As a refresher: El Niño is characterized by warmer-than-average water temperatures along the equator in the Pacific Ocean. The warmer water triggers corresponding shifts in the atmosphere that have a domino effect on weather patterns around the globe. An active Pacific hurricane season that’s churned out multiple threats for Hawaii, a hurricane-less Atlantic hurricane season to date and Indonesia’s overwhelming wildfires are just a few effects of this very strong El Niño. The stronger an El Niño is, the more likely it is to influence these types of weather patterns — but it doesn’t guarantee more extreme impacts. Turning super To capture El Niño’s strength, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration forecasters measure how far above normal sea surface temperatures are in a specific region of the Pacific, using a metric called the Niño 3.4 Relative Oceanic Niño Index, or RONI. The latest weekly RONI value just hit 2.0 degrees Celsius, 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, above average. This is the threshold for “very strong,” the highest official category set by forecasters. That’s also when El Niño gains its unofficial “super” moniker. These weekly values from NOAA capture a reliable snapshot of El Niño’s strength in real-time, which is crucial because of just how fast the event is gaining ground. This time a year ago, a weak La Niña — El Niño’s cool counterpart — was in place, and only a handful of other years have had such a rapid flip to a potent El Niño, including the strongest ever event from 1982 to 1983. Even so, using the weekly values is a slight departure from the norm. NOAA’s most widely recognized strength metric is a three-month rolling average RONI. The rolling average’s purpose is to smooth out choppy short-term changes in data in favor of capturing a cleaner long-term average; that value updates once a month. This is how a climate record that dates back decades is built, but the delayed data means it’ll take weeks for that reading to truly capture how super-sized El Niño is right now. Breaking new ground This isn’t a normal event: In addition to being the strongest El Niño on record on this date, it’s ultimately likely to become stronger than any event before it. By the end of the year, El Niño has a 75% chance of peaking as the strongest event since records began in 1950, according to NOAA’s latest forecast issued last week. This year’s El Niño is also happening in a much hotter world than previous record-setting events due to climate change. One look at sea surface temperatures from this year compared to past record events shows just how much fossil fuel pollution has rewritten the rules. Climate change has literally changed the metric used to monitor El Niño. This event is the first to be captured by NOAA’s aforementioned RONI, which was first implemented in February. The old metric took sea surface temperatures at face value, but RONI subtracts out how much warmer the Pacific Ocean is because of climate change to get the “true” strength of El Niño. Even so, this El Niño continues to clear hurdles in its pursuit of record-breaking strength later this fall or early this winter. Past, present and still to come Winter is when El Niño is forecast to hit its peak strength and is also typically when its influence on global weather is most pronounced, but it’s already left many calling cards behind this summer as it strengthened rapidly. It was, and continues to be, a major factor in both the Atlantic and Pacific hurricane seasons. In the Atlantic, it’s taken storm-killing wind shear to extreme levels and kept it there, even at what should be the busiest time of the season. That’s created a record-long wait for the season’s first hurricane. El Niño has prevented that same type of wind shear over the exceptionally warm Pacific and activity exploded. Sixteen storms, including two Category 5 hurricanes, have formed and thrived in the eastern and central parts of the ocean so far, with Hawaii alone facing three tropical systems in less than a month. Fourteen of those storms originated in the East Pacific, which, with two and a half months of the season still to come, will likely blow past its average seasonal storm total of 15. Elsewhere, Indonesia is battling widespread wildfires and conditions could deteriorate further: El Niño years make the country drier than usual, which leaves plenty of tinder-dry vegetation for blazes to consume and limited rainfall to help fire crews tamp down ongoing activity. El Niño also raises global average air temperatures above levels already being increased by climate change and was a factor in making this summer such a scorcher around the globe. This August was Earth’s hottest on record and could mark the start of a record-breaking warm stretch that would likely culminate in a record-hot 2027 — and possibly 2026 — globally. It’s clear El Niño is already a major player, but it will hit its full stride in the months ahead, right on time to dictate winter weather across the US.

articles.title: Cooling towers at Yankee Stadium test positive for Legionnaires’ in new cluster
articles.summary: The New York City Health Department has ordered 10 cooling towers in the South Bronx to be cleaned and disinfected after preliminary testing found the presence of Legionella bacteria as officials investigate a cluster in ZIP codes 10451 and 10456.
articles.body: The New York City Health Department has ordered 10 cooling towers in the South Bronx to be cleaned and disinfected after preliminary testing found the presence of Legionella bacteria as officials investigate a cluster in ZIP codes 10451 and 10456. Two of the locations are tied to high-profile sites: one cooling tower is at Yankee Stadium, 1 E. 161st St., where the Yankees played the Mets in the Subway Series on Sunday, and another is at 234 E. 149th St., the address of Lincoln Hospital. The Boricua College Bronx Campus is 890 Washington Ave. is also among the sites. NYC officials on Sunday said there are now nine confirmed cases connected to the cluster; three people were hospitalized and one person has died. Mandatory cleaning and disinfection of the 10 cooling towers is expected to be finished by Monday, the health department said. The 10 towers tested positive for the presence of Legionella bacteria through an initial PCR (polymerase chain reaction) test. “The one limitation, the one thing wrong with the PCR test, is it can’t tell us if the DNA is live legionella or dead,” NYC Health Commissioner Dr. Alister Martin explained in a virtual town hall for people in the Melrose and Morrisania neighborhoods Sunday. “And so, some of those 10 might have live bacteria, some of those might have dead bacteria, and it’s only the live bacteria that can get you sick.” The city said it is also conducting culture testing to determine whether live Legionella bacteria were present when the samples were collected, but that results can take up to two weeks. The 10 cooling towers with positive PCR results are located at: 820 Concourse Village West234 E. 149th St.1 E. 161st St.470 E. 161st St.1265 Franklin Ave.567 Melrose Ave.3339 Park Ave.1160 Teller Ave.890 Washington Ave.1085 Washington Ave. In all, the city has inspected 24 cooling towers as part of the investigation. The probe began after the NYC Department of Health identified a cluster of Legionnaires’ disease cases in Melrose and Morrisania, which are part of ZIP codes 10451 and 10456. Anyone who lives, works, or has visited the area since late August and develops flu-like symptoms should contact a health care provider immediately. Authorities said it is safe to shower, drink tap water and use air conditioners in the affected ZIP codes unless otherwise advised, and that there is no additional risk from being inside any of the 10 buildings with cooling towers that tested positive for the presence of Legionella bacteria. The Health Department will host an in-person town hall at 6 p.m. Tuesday at Metropolitan College in the Bronx. This story was originally reported for broadcast by NBC New York. AI tools helped convert the story to a digital article, and an NBC New York journalist edited the article for publication.

articles.title: Why Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline matters for global oil
articles.summary: The 1,200km (745-mile) pipeline has been temporarily closed, affecting up to 5 percent of global oil supply.
articles.body:
In another blow to global oil markets, drones struck Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline last Thursday, prompting the kingdom to suspend operations.

The 1,200km (746-mile) pipeline, which carries roughly 4 to 5 million barrels of oil per day (bpd), links the country’s major oil-producing fields in the east with the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which has largely been closed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran in February.

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said the shutdown was a “precautionary” measure after the attack caused damage and injuries in the Riyadh and Medina regions.

The closure comes as the US-Israel war on Iran has sharply reduced oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi forces in Yemen have intensified attacks around the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb.

With oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz severely disrupted, Saudi Arabia has relied more heavily on the East-West pipeline. What does its closure mean for an already tight global oil market?

The extent of the damage is not yet clear, and estimates of how quickly the pipeline can return to normal operations vary. Sources familiar with the incident told the Reuters news agency that repairs could take five to six weeks, while another source said operations could restart sooner.

Saudi officials said drones hit the pipeline in two areas around Riyadh and Medina. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the attack caused injuries and damage to infrastructure.

According to Saudi authorities, the launch of the drones was traced to Maysan province in southeastern Iraq, close to the Iranian border and an area where Iran-aligned armed groups have established a longstanding presence.

The attack follows a strike in March near the Saudi-Aramco-ExxonMobil refinery in Yanbu that temporarily disrupted crude loadings from the Red Sea port. That incident had little lasting impact on operations, with shipments recovering within days, but it demonstrated that the kingdom’s western oil infrastructure was not immune to attacks.

The East-West pipeline, also known as the Petroline, is a 1,200km (745-mile) long oil pipeline built in 1981 that carries crude oil from the kingdom’s eastern oil fields near Abqaiq across the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

It has a maximum capacity of seven million bpd, although actual flows have been lower in recent months – about two million bpd in August according to Kpler – the lowest monthly level since January as Houthi attacks made the Red Sea route difficult to use.

Saudi Arabia increased the amount of crude sent west during the first five months of the conflict, taking flows to roughly 4-5 million bpd. That represents about 4 to 5 percent of global supply and allowed the world’s second largest oil exporter to bypass the Strait of Hormuz when shipping conditions deteriorated.

The pipeline’s closure comes at a critical point for the global oil market.

Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz supplied more than a fifth of oil globally – about 20 million bpd. According to Reuters, industry estimates now put the flow at about 6-9 million bpd through the strait, a dramatic reduction in the volume.

Saudi Arabia has responded by moving more crude towards the Red Sea. However, the flow and export of that oil depends on the pipeline, storage facilities and tankers transiting safely – all of which have been made vulnerable since the Iran war began in February.

According to sources close to Reuters, if the pipeline remains shut, Yanbu has enough available stocks to sustain exports for about five to seven days, while Egyptian facilities in Ain Sukhna and Sidi Kerir, which store Saudi oil, could provide additional supplies for several days.

While this gives Saudi Arabia some buffer, it comes as global inventories have already been falling. The International Energy Agency said Saudi oil supply reached a more than three-decade low in August, with disruptions in Hormuz and the Red Sea. It says world oil supplies will decline by some 5.7 million bpd this year, equivalent to 6 percent of global supply.

Oil prices have so far been cushioned by stockpiles and releases from strategic reserves, with Brent crude trading about $70-$90 in recent months. But the longer regional disruptions continue, the more those reserves will be depleted and the higher prices will rise.

In June, the IEA said continued drawdowns could hit critical levels with experts saying that if inventories approach exceptionally low levels, Brent could potentially rise to $150 a barrel.

If damage to the pipeline proves extensive, and attacks continue to threaten Yanbu and shipping routes beyond it, Saudi Arabia could find that its ability to compensate for lost Gulf exports is itself becoming constrained.

Gavekal Research noted that if Yanbu, which processes more than one million bpd, goes offline because of threats from Houthi drones, “this would be a disaster for the world at a time when global refining capacity is already critically tight.”

articles.title: Portadown: No police collusion in Robert Hamill murder but multiple RUC failings included tip-off to suspect
articles.summary: Robert Hamill died after he was beaten by loyalists in Portadown, County Armagh.
articles.body:
An inquiry into the sectarian murder of Robert Hamill has found police officers who were in a vehicle near the attack did not condone or collude with the attackers.

However, the inquiry said there were multiple police failings in the investigation, including a tip-off to a suspect to destroy the clothing he wore that night.

The report, published on Monday , highlighted multiple wrongful omissions in the subsequent murder investigation including a failure to properly search the home of a key suspect.

Robert Hamill was 25 when he died after he was beaten by loyalists in Portadown, County Armagh, in 1997.

The inquiry concluded in 2009 and its report was completed in 2011 but the findings could not be published until three prosecutions in connection with the case concluded.

The inquiry concluded: "We find that Robert Hamill had been assaulted before the Land Rover officers got out of their vehicle.

"However, they were not aware of the assault and after they had got out of their vehicle, they attempted to restore order.

"They did not in any way condone or collude with attackers."

Although the inquiry found that the four officers in the police Land Rover could not have prevented the murder, the police investigation was flawed – both at the scene and in the days that followed.

"The inquiry found that serving RUC [Royal Ulster Constabulary] officers were guilty of wrongful omissions and that those omissions arose both at the scene and during the initial investigation," it said.

The inquiry concluded that some of the mistakes in the investigation were negligent, while others were deliberate.

The 290-page report followed an inquiry which cost approximately £33m.

The actions of the officers in the Land Rover have been the subject of many claims and counter-claims in the past three decades.

Given how close they were to the scene, questions have been asked about why they did not intervene sooner.

The inquiry found that they were "distracted talking to two members of the public".

On whether they could have done more, the three-person inquiry panel did not have a unanimous view.

Two members concluded that the officers in the police vehicle were not guilty "of any wrongful act or omission in relation to the death of Robert Hamill".

However, on this issue the chairperson Sir Edwin Jowitt "expressed a dissenting view".

The inquiry report identified a number of key mistakes in the police investigation.

Failure to keep full records of the investigation

Failure to properly search home of a key suspect

Failure to carry out full debriefing of officers at scene of attack

Nobody has been convicted of the murder.

Speaking after the report's publication, Hamill's sister Diane said the family had "some reservations about aspects of this report".

"We as a family feel totally vindicated by the clear and unequivocal findings of the panel," she said.

"It documents multiple and shocking wrongdoing, some of it delivered by state agencies.

"These failings have led to those who murdered our brother evading justice."

She added that the family was "disappointed" that the panel could not agree "on the consequences of the police officers in the Land Rover failing to intervene while Robert was being attacked".

"I just want to reiterate that the people who killed our brother were never fully held accountable due to the obstructive conduct of the state justice agencies," she said.

In terms of deliberate mistakes, the actions of now-retired RUC officer Robert Atkinson were highlighted.

The inquiry found he was "guilty of a wrongful act" for making a telephone call to the home of a suspect.

The report said this resulted in that individual "destroying or putting beyond the reach of police the clothes he had been wearing that night".

"This obstructed the investigation and was deliberate," stated the report.

It said Atkinson subsequently conspired to cover up the "tip-off telephone call".

This was "an obstruction of the murder investigation and was deliberate" according to the three-person inquiry panel.

Northern Ireland Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said it is "especially disturbing" that Atkinson "carried an RUC badge for years when he had so evidently and heinously failed in his duty and acted as an criminal".

Sir Chris added that it is "difficult not to agree" that there was a "catalogue of failures".

He said the report's publication is a reminder of the "long shadow of the troubles" and how other families "yearn for answers about how their loved ones were killed".

"He would have been coming up to his 55th birthday in December - younger than me," Sir Chris said in the House of Commons on Monday.

"He might have become a grandfather or a great uncle by now but he was murdered and murdered just for being a Catholic."

The former Police Ombudsman Baroness Nuala O'Loan told BBC's Evening Extra programme there had been a "pattern of failures to investigate".

Hamill and a friend were attacked and beaten by loyalists as they walked along Portadown's Market Street after a night out in April 1997.

He suffered serious head injuries and died 11 days later.

Hamill's murder was the subject of a public inquiry because it was alleged officers were parked in a police Land Rover nearby but did not intervene.

That inquiry ran for 77 days between 13 January and 17 December 2009.

It heard evidence in person from 174 witnesses and witness statements from a further 37 witnesses.

No one was convicted of the murder and in the decades after, Hamill's family demanded answers.

The sectarian killing happened at time when tensions were high in Northern Ireland.

While peace talks were under way, the Drumcree parade dispute in Portadown in the 1990s sparked some of the most serious public disorder in Northern Ireland's history.

Timeline: What happened after Robert Hamill's murder?

The attack happened in the early hours of Sunday 27 April 1997.

At about 01:20 BST he left a dance at St Patrick's Hall and walked towards the town centre.

Different versions of events have been given for what happened next.

The inquiry stated: "Almost everything else that happened between the time when Robert Hamill left St Patrick's Hall and the time he was put into the ambulance is a matter of dispute."

However, the inquiry was in no doubt he was murdered.

The report stated: "Those who assaulted him must have at least intended to cause him serious injury."

It added: "Robert Hamill suffered head trauma either shortly after that violence broke out or a little later when…Protestant youths kicked him while he was on the ground."

articles.title: A West Virginia family with roots around Audra stretching back 175 years donated 47 acres to the state park; one gift increases the entire park by about 13%
articles.summary: US News: A West Virginia family with ties to the Audra area for over 175 years donated 47 acres to Audra State Park. In September, the Thacker family signed ov.
articles.body: A West Virginia family with ties to the Audra area for over 175 years donated 47 acres to Audra State Park. In September, the Thacker family signed over the property at the state Capitol, along with a $15,000 donation for trails and signs on the new property, known as the Thacker Addition, according to a report by West Virginia Explorer News. This is a significant boost for a modest park nestled between two counties in the Appalachian foothills.With this generous donation, Audra State Park will expand from its previous 355 acres to roughly 402 acres. For a relatively small state park, this expansion is substantial. The donated land alone is larger than the 44 acres the state added to the park in 1961.A generous donation with family tiesOn September 3, the family of Victor and Mary Thacker formally donated their property in a ceremonial deed signing at the West Virginia State Capitol. The Thacker family made the donation in honour of Victor Thacker’s great-great-grandparents, Jacob Johnson Thacker and Sarah Ann DeMasters Thacker. These 47 acres of land will provide space for future trail development, according to officials.‘West Virginia State Parks is deeply grateful for this extraordinary gift from the Thacker family,’ Dillard Price, acting chief of West Virginia State Parks, said.He called the generous donation an investment in the state's natural and cultural heritage. ‘Each acre our state parks protect represents a lasting investment in our state’s natural, cultural and historical resources — a gift that directly benefits future generations.’The Thacker family's foothold in Barbour County, where the park sits, goes back nearly two centuries. While park officials did not specify whether the donated land itself stayed in family hands throughout those 175 years, the gift points to the family’s enduring ties to the region.Audra itself traces back to a small river community that emerged around the 20th century. By then, five families occupied the spot along the Middle Fork, according to the West Virginia Encyclopedia. A gristmill and sawmill anchored the settlement in those early years. The landscape around it was logged; later, Barbour County 4-H groups used the area as a camp between 1919 and 1923. Later, the state acquired the property. Audra State Park formally opened in 1950, with additional acreage added over the following decade as the park took shape. Today, it is known chiefly for the river gorge, the forest canopy and those established trails. With the Thacker family's 47-acre donation, the park will see an extension without erasing any of its past.More room to roamAudra State Park stretches across Barbour and Upshur counties along the Middle Fork River, a landscape of forested hillsides tumbling towards a rocky corridor, making it a popular destination for outdoor recreation, especially among hikers, swimmers and anglers.The park's signature hiking route is the Alum Cave Trail, a 2.7-mile loop that follows the Middle Fork through thick forest and beneath a distinctive sandstone overhang known as Alum Cave. West Virginia State Parks also lists a shorter trail called the Rock Cliff Trail. The Thacker Addition opens possibilities for expanding those options, though park officials have not yet released designs for the new trails the funding will support. Officials have also not revealed the location of the new plot, and it is unknown whether it includes river frontage. Regardless, this additional land will create more opportunities for hiking at the park. Park officials have not announced final designs for the trails yet. However, this generous donation means future visitors to Audra will have more ground to explore, more of the river gorge to hike and more reasons to return.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Alaska teen rescued after 3 days in frigid waters reveals tragic end for 2 family members
articles.summary: Derek Parker Aghnaanga, 15, clung to a capsized skiff for two days in the Bering Sea near St. Lawrence Island before a Coast Guard crew spotted him.
articles.body: An Alaska teenager who survived nearly two days atop an overturned fishing skiff told his rescuers that his cousin had slipped away during the night and that his older brother remained beneath the vessel after the three were thrown into the frigid Bering Sea, according to rescuers and family members. Derek Parker Aghnaanga, 15, was spotted Monday morning on the capsized skiff roughly four miles east of St. Lawrence Island after he, his 35-year-old brother Sidney Kulowiyi and their cousin disappeared during a fishing trip. "Through the teeth chattering, he had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff," Adam White, captain of the fishing vessel Northwest Explorer, told Anchorage affiliate KTUU-TV. "And then he said that, in the previous night, before our rescue, that his cousin had slipped away." A GoFundMe page organized by relatives said Aghnaanga tried to hold onto his brother and cousin after they died, before their bodies were recovered. TRAGEDY AT SEA LEAVES TEEN STRANDED ON OVERTURNED BOAT FOR NEARLY 3 DAYS IN FRIGID WATERS A U.S. Coast Guard HC-130 Hercules aircrew from Air Station Kodiak spotted Aghnaanga atop the overturned vessel and dropped a survival raft and equipment before deploying flares to guide the Northwest Explorer to his location. Crew members aboard the Northwest Explorer pulled Aghnaanga to safety and recovered the bodies of Kulowiyi and the teenager's cousin. Aghnaanga was experiencing symptoms of hypothermia when he was rescued. Crew members wrapped him in blankets and used hot packs to warm him as the vessel transported him to Nome. The three had departed the remote Alaska Native village of Savoonga on Friday for a fishing trip and planned to return early Sunday. Family members reported them missing Sunday night, prompting a search involving the Coast Guard, Alaska State Troopers and other state and local agencies. MISSING 70-YEAR-OLD HIKER RESCUED AFTER DISAPPEARING FOR A WEEK IN REMOTE NATIONAL PARK Colleen Walker, an aunt of the brothers, described Kulowiyi as a humble commercial fishing captain and provider for Savoonga, a village of roughly 800 residents where halibut fishing remains an important part of community life. "We all cried and jumped for joy when the captain announced on the radio, 'We found a kid, he's alive, he's alive,'" Walker told The Associated Press, describing family members listening to the rescue effort. Kulowiyi left behind children, according to the family fundraiser, which had raised more than $42,000 toward a $45,000 goal as of Monday morning. "Our hearts go out to the families, friends, and communities affected by the tragic loss of these two mariners," Rear Adm. Bob Little, commander of the Coast Guard Arctic District, said in a statement. The Coast Guard Arctic District coordinated the search with the Alaska Rescue Coordination Center, the Alaska Air National Guard's 176th Wing, Alaska State Troopers and local authorities in Savoonga. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP Neither the Coast Guard nor Alaska State Troopers have said what caused the skiff to capsize.

articles.title: Allow Canadians to live and work in Europe without a visa: Mark Carney discusses possibility of closer ties with EU countries amid tensions with US
articles.summary: Europe News: Canada is exploring a much closer relationship with the European Union amid its worsening trade and political tensions with the US, with reports sugge.
articles.body: Canada is exploring a much closer relationship with the European Union amid its worsening trade and political tensions with the US, with reports suggesting Ottawa is considering a new form of “associate membership” with the bloc. The proposal, reported by The Wall Street Journal, would seek deeper economic and strategic integration between Canada and the EU without Canada becoming a full EU member.However, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has stressed that Canada is not seeking EU membership. He has described the proposed relationship as a “unique alliance” based on shared values, priorities and strengths.The idea is significant because a closer relationship could eventually make it easier for Canadians to do business, work, study and potentially move between Canada and European countries.For now, however, Canadians remain non-EU nationals and do not have the automatic right to settle in any EU country."Wouldn’t it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?" asked Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who speaks regularly with Carney, as reported by WSJ.Can Canadians currently move to Europe and settle?Not simply because they are Canadian.Canadian passport holders can travel to countries in the Schengen area without a visa for short stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. That is a visitor entitlement, not a right to live or work permanently in Europe.A Canadian who wants to stay in an EU country for longer than 90 days generally has to obtain the appropriate long-stay visa or residence permit from that country.The rules are decided largely at the national level. The European Union itself does not issue a single “EU residence visa” that allows a Canadian to simply settle anywhere in the bloc. The European Commission specifically says applications for visas and residence permits must be made directly to the authorities of the EU country where the person intends to move.That means a Canadian wanting to move to France, Germany, Spain, Italy or another EU country has to qualify under that country's immigration system.How can a Canadian currently settle in an EU country?The route depends on the individual's circumstances.A Canadian may qualify for residence through employment, study, family reunification, highly skilled work, entrepreneurship or other national immigration programmes.For example, a Canadian who receives a qualifying job offer in an EU country may be able to obtain a work visa or residence permit. A student can apply for a student residence permit, while a person joining a qualifying family member can use family-reunification rules.EU immigration rules cover categories including highly qualified workers, intra-company transferees, seasonal workers, researchers and students, but individual EU countries make the final decision on applications.A Canadian who legally lives in an EU country for a sufficiently long period may eventually qualify for long-term resident status. Under EU rules applicable in most member states, a non-EU national who has legally resided in an EU country for five years may be eligible for long-term resident status, subject to conditions such as sufficient financial resources and health insurance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Jeremy Lin: The 6-year-old Perth musician who won sole first prize in his age group and became the youngest performer on a Carnegie Hall program
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At just six years old, Perth musician Jeremy Lin has already performed at one of the world’s most celebrated concert venues. The Christ Church Grammar.
articles.body: At just six years old, Perth musician Jeremy Lin has already performed at one of the world’s most celebrated concert venues. The Christ Church Grammar School Pre-Primary student won the Gold Award and the sole First Prize in Group A at the fifth PREMIA International Young Artists Music Festival, competing against performers aged four to six. His achievement earned him an invitation to the prizewinners concert at Weill Recital Hall at Carnegie Hall in New York, where he became the youngest musician on the programme. As reported by Christ Church Grammar School, Jeremy’s performance was judged by a 24-member international jury, turning an early childhood interest in music into an extraordinary international milestone.A remarkable beginningMost six-year-olds are still discovering what they enjoy. Some are experimenting with sport, drawing, reading or music, while others are simply learning how to concentrate on a task for longer periods. Jeremy’s experience shows what can happen when talent, practice and opportunity come together at an early age. His journey began in Perth, where he attends Christ Church Grammar School. He has been developing his musical ability as a Pre-Primary student, participating in school life and sharing his interest with classmates. The school says Jeremy is an excellent musician who enjoys playing both the piano and the violin. Remarkably, he plays both instruments because the two instruments require different physical skills and approaches. The piano requires co-ordination of both hands across a keyboard, while the violin requires posture, bow control and the ability to produce a clear tone without frets. Mastering one instrument can be demanding for a young performer. Developing confidence across two suggests that Jeremy is comfortable exploring different ways of expressing himself musically.PREMIA festival competitionEarlier in 2026, Jeremy entered the fifth PREMIA International Young Artists Music Festival. He competed in Group A, which was open to performers aged four to six. Competitions at this age are not only about technical performance. Young musicians must also manage the unfamiliar experience of playing before judges and an audience. They need to remember the music, recover if something goes wrong and remain focused despite the pressure of the setting. Jeremy’s playing impressed a 24-member international jury. The judges awarded him the Gold Award and the sole First Prize in his category. The result meant he was not simply one of several highly commended performers. He was the only first prize winner in Group A.The award also demonstrated that his performance connected with experienced musicians from different backgrounds. An international jury brings a broad range of expectations and listening experiences, making the recognition especially meaningful for a young performer.An invitation to Carnegie HallThe first prize came with an invitation to perform at the PREMIA International Young Artists Music Festival Prizewinners Concert. The event took place at Weill Recital Hall at Carnegie Hall in New York. Carnegie Hall has a long association with major musical performances. The venue has welcomed musicians including The Beatles, Louis Armstrong and Elton John. For professional performers, appearing there can represent the culmination of years of work. For Jeremy, the invitation arrived while he was still in Pre-Primary. Weill Recital Hall is one of Carnegie Hall’s performance spaces and is known for chamber music, recitals and emerging artists. Performing there placed Jeremy in a setting with a strong musical history and an audience prepared to listen closely. The concert also brought together prizewinners from the festival. Jeremy was the youngest musician on the programme, making his appearance especially distinctive. He was not simply attending the event as a young audience member. He was performing as one of the recognised artists.What it takes to perform so youngA six-year-old musician still has a developing attention span, memory and ability to manage nerves. Preparing for an international performance requires careful support from teachers and family members. Young children learn differently from adults. Repetition needs to be balanced with play, and practice sessions must be structured around the child’s energy and concentration. Encouragement is as important as correction, for confidence can affect the quality of a performance. For Jeremy, the Carnegie Hall appearance would have been more than not learning notes. He would have had to travel across the world, adapt to another environment and perform in a very prestigious setting. The experience may have been unfamiliar acoustics, a different piano and the emotional pressure of being observed by an audience. These challenges can become valuable parts of musical education. A child who learns how to prepare, travel and perform may develop skills that continue to help in future competitions and concerts.Piano and violin as creative toolsJeremy’s interest in both piano and violin gives him different ways to understand music. The piano is a clear visual layout, with notes laid out across the keyboard, and multiple pitches available at once. It can provide harmony, melody and rhythm in a single performance. The violin is more physically direct. The sound is produced by the player through the relationship of bow, strings and fingers. The pitch is determined by precise placement and the performer needs to listen continuously to adjust tone and intonation. Learning both instruments can enhance musical awareness. A student may begin to recognise how melody moves between instruments or how different sounds can express the same musical idea. It can also encourage flexibility, as the performer learns to adapt technique to the instrument. For Jeremy, the combination appears to be part of a broader love of music rather than a narrow focus on competition. His school has described him as someone who enjoys performing and sharing creative ideas with peers.The role of school supportA young musician’s achievement is personal, but it rarely happens without a supportive network. Teachers provide guidance, families create time for practice, and schools offer encouragement and opportunities to perform. Christ Church Grammar School celebrated Jeremy’s Carnegie Hall appearance as a significant achievement for the school community. Being recognised by teachers and classmates is a way to help a young performer to see that music is not just an individual activity. It can also be a way to connect with others. School communities offer an audience that is familiar and encouraging. Performing for classmates can help a child build confidence before appearing in a formal competition or international concert. It also allows peers to see the effort that goes into the result. Jeremy’s success may inspire other students to explore music, whether through piano, violin or another instrument. A visible example can make performance feel more accessible and show that serious musicianship can begin during the early years of schooling.More than a trophyTo win the Gold Award and First Prize is an amazing achievement, but the real value of this journey is more than a trophy or a certificate. For Jeremy, it is a rare chance to go out on an international stage, meet other young musicians and soak up the magic of a world-famous concert hall. Moments like this completely change a child’s view of music. Playing a piece isn’t just a classroom exercise anymore; it becomes tied to travel, history, and a much bigger, global community of artists. Standing on the stage at Carnegie Hall is the kind of memory that stays vivid for a lifetime, no matter where his love for music takes him down the road.Beyond the spotlight, competitions teach grit. Every artist hits off-notes, and no one wins first place every single time. Learning to take constructive feedback in stride, stick to the practice routine, and actually love the process builds character that matters way more than a shelf full of awards. At just six years old, Jeremy has endless time to explore new instruments and discover his own style. This early win is a wonderful spark, but it’s only the first chapter of his story.A milestone in a young musical lifeJeremy’s Carnegie Hall appearance is remarkable because of the combination of age, achievement and setting. He won the sole First Prize in his age group, earned an invitation to a prizewinners concert and became the youngest performer on the programme. Yet the most human part of the story is simple. A young child who enjoys music had the opportunity to perform for a large audience in a place known around the world. His achievement reflects talent and preparation, but also the joy of discovering something he wants to share. As Jeremy continues to work on his piano and violin skills, this performance at Carnegie Hall will be just one chapter in a longer musical journey. It could lead to more competitions, concerts or other interests altogether. Whatever comes next, the experience has already shown him his music can go far beyond his classroom in Perth.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Nigel Farage says £72m donation are compliant 'with the law today'
articles.summary: Ministers are seeking to put a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British expats, backdated to 25 March 2026.
articles.body:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has said two big donations given to his party are "100% compliant with the law today", but was not able say whether they would be permissible if a rule change, currently being debated in Parliament, were passed.

Ministers are seeking to put a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British expats, backdated to 25 March 2026.

Farage argued the government should not retrospectively declare donations illegal and threatened to retaliate by limiting trade union donations, if elected PM.

Trade union leader Paul Nowak said there was no similarity between "care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union and a party bought and paid for by billionaires."

Over the weekend, Reform announced that it had received two donations of £36m each from wealthy businessmen Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British but have until recently lived abroad.

Speaking to the BBC, Farage said there was "no question" their donations - the largest in British political history - were within the law "as it stands".

Asked if the two men were resident in the UK by 25 March, Farage said: "I'm not going into their particular details."

He went on to criticise the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal, saying: "This cannot be."

"If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way.

"We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'."

Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

Donations law changes to be debated after Reform's £72m windfall

Will record donations to Reform go down as a moment of political change?

Who is Reform donor and crypto billionaire Ben Delo?

The House of Lords is currently debating the government's Representation of the People Bill which caps the amount British people living overseas can donate to political parties at £100,000.

The bill also states that those who moved back to the UK would have to wait for at least a year before donating more than £100,000.

The legislation states that donors must have been registered as in the UK by 25 March 2026 in order to avoid the cap.

It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK.

Education Minister Georgia Gould told the BBC's Today programme the government was "really worried about the big money that is coming into politics... and sometimes money from overseas that is shaping politics rather than the ordinary voters".

She said the new rule changes had been added to the bill, following a report by former senior civil servant Sir Philip Rycroft into foreign interference in British politics, published on 25 March.

The two £36m donations to Reform have reignited questions about political funding.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on Radio 5 Live, Sir Philip said examining domestic donations had not been within the remit of his review but that there was a case for capping all donations, whether they came from British citizens living in the UK or overseas.

"I don't see any reason why we should have these mega sums of money coming into British politics," he said.

He added that the government's decision to retrospectively ban certain donations was "going to be controversial" but said: "If you say, you're going to change the rules to cap donations at some point in the future, then clearly the risk is that you get a lot of those donations coming through the door before you're able to do that."

Farage said the donations would allow his party to "catch up with the other big parties" and enable them to "professionalise".

He argued that trade unions gave money to Labour so that it would enact their policies and that donors gave money to the Conservative Party in order to get "knighthoods and peerages".

By contrast he said neither Harborne or Delo would get peerages or government contracts, if Reform won the next general election.

Asked if the two men had influence over Reform's policy on cryptocurrency, Farage said he had shown them his party's paper on the subject and they both "thought it made sense".

He added that the two men "will not benefit" from Reform's policies, which he said aimed to properly regulate cryptocurrency.

Farage was speaking on the same day as the Trade Unions Congress, the federation of trade unions, held its annual conference.

TUC general secretary Nowak said Reform were a "party for sale" and their donations were "a crisis for democracy".

Sharon Graham, leader of the Unite union, said the government should go further and put a cap between £500,000 and £1m on individual donations made by UK residents

Speaking on Sunday, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending. Similarly, the Green Party urged the Labour Party to "find its spine and support a tight cap".

articles.title: Russia’s drone strike near Ukraine-Poland border puts NATO neighbors on edge
articles.summary: It doesn’t really matter if they meant to do it. Russia’s drone strike on a train in Ukraine that the railway network said likely targeted foreign officials is a clear escalation.
articles.body: It doesn’t really matter if they meant to do it. The Russian drone strike that hit a train near Ukraine’s border with Poland as a group of former Western officials travelled out of the country is a clear escalation by Moscow. Ukraine’s railway network said it believes former CIA chief David Petraeus, former UK prime minister Boris Johnson and other dignitaries who were all nearby, either at the local railway station or on trains, were likely targeted. Intent is hard to prove in conflict. The proof, to some degree, is an afterthought in the rubble – the damage is by then clear, as is the need for retaliation. Killing a former CIA chief on a railway platform would have provided some element of deniability for Russia; how could they know for sure he was there? But it would fulfil the warnings of Western intelligence, circulating for some time now, that Moscow will seek some form of escalation with Ukraine’s NATO allies in the near future. A full-on military conflict with NATO seemed an unlikely goal for a Russian state struggling to suppress and occupy its relatively tiny neighbor. Instead, a lateral move, in the deniable hybrid space, seemed more likely, and Ukraine and others warned its borders with NATO states might come under attack. The immediate impact of Ukraine’s diplomatic commuter link being under attack is profound. The railway is the best method for heads of state or senior officials from Ukraine’s allies to get in and out of Kyiv, to show vital support, share the most sensitive intelligence, or discuss vital matters. Trains, and the civilians on them, now routinely come under attack from Russian drones. The latest versions use other airborne Russian drones to transmit signals and even video feeds, in real time, back to their pilots inside Russia. These “mesh” networks extend their range and lessen the risk electronic warfare can disrupt them, a remarkable development that helped Moscow hit trains so close to Poland. The net result is Western officials and their security details, whose job it is to minimize risk, must now either rethink how they get in and out of Ukraine or widen the envelope of acceptable risk. In a wartorn country where air travel is too perilous to even consider, the roads are the obvious option, but are jammed, precarious, and cursed with long, torturous border queues. New ideas are needed to maintain the flow of high-profile visitors to Kyiv at a time when shows of support, real aid, and proper partnership are essential. It is likely that without the option of a swift and safe railway, Western officials facing a longer trip time than about 10 hours each way will reconsider whether a remote video call isn’t just better. This is likely part of Russia’s aim – to deny Ukraine the easy and free use of its border crossings and rail network to move goods and important visitors, and to leave its Western neighbors on edge. Moscow’s drip-drip escalation has been palpable for years now, as sabotage incidents become more frequent, and recklessness in the form of stray drones or ballistic missiles cross into and test NATO’s outer defenses. None of this sustained probing is accidental. It all fits inside Russia’s grey-zone doctrine of conflict, in which heightening confrontation happens in gradual, tiny steps, none of which, in themselves, appear worth starting a war over. But the picture is increasingly bleak for NATO and, of course, Ukraine. Moscow correctly calculates that NATO – fractured between the Trump administration and Europe and partially distracted with Iran – does not have the bandwidth or budget for proper conflict with a Kremlin that believes winning – or even sustaining - this war in some way is a matter of survival. Similarly, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin lacks the resources to risk a full-on war with NATO. But his military-industrial base is slowly edging into a new era of cheaper, longer-range, more accurate and deadly drones and missiles. The new Russian jet-powered Geran 4 and 5 drones travel at 600 kilometers (373 miles) an hour over 1,000 kilometers. Ukraine struggles to stop them, and its engineers are working on the issue 24/7 as a matter of life and death. For NATO, they represent a future horror that European member states hope never comes their way, given that their military spending on the technology they would need to defend themselves is, to be polite, uselessly behind the curve. Ukrainians already face a winter blighted by heightened attacks on heating and food supplies. That is guaranteed, especially as the West has failed to supply them with more Patriot interceptors. The fresh struggle of the coming months will be for NATO to tackle Moscow’s growing reach, daring and persistence, when it comes to threatening their borders, former prime ministers on railways, and probably border crossing points too. The warnings of escalation have amplified for months. With Sunday’s railway attack, the moment of their realization is upon a poorly-equipped Western alliance.

articles.title: Top Oversight Democrat wants answers on Russian oligarch’s role in Trump Jr.’s wedding
articles.summary: Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the ranking member on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, pressed for answers on a Russian oligarch’s reported role in a wedding for one of President Trump’s sons. According to a report published Monday by ProPublica, Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding in May received funding from Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev, who…
articles.body:
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the ranking member on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, pressed for answers on a Russian oligarch’s reported role in a wedding for one of President Trump’s sons.

According to a report published Monday by ProPublica, Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding in May received funding from Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev, who is linked to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The outlet reported that the oligarch paid for Trump Jr.’s wedding expenses in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, citing records and three sources with knowledge of the event. For the president’s son’s big event, ProPublica reported, Kremlev helped rent an island and put up the money for a fireworks show.

“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?” Garcia wrote on social media Monday morning in a response to the ProPublica report.

“Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers,” he added.

Last December , Trump Jr. said that he was engaged at the White House holiday party in front of family, friends and guests. The president’s son called his engagement to Bettina Anderson, a Palm Beach, Fla., socialite, a “big win” for the end of 2025.

Trump Jr.’s wife, who now goes by Bettina Trump, clapped back at the ProPublica report in an Instagram post on Monday , saying that she and her husband “got married privately on” May 22, “surrounded ONLY by our family.”

“Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” she added later.

The Hill has reached out to Kremlev for comment.

articles.title: Key convicted Palestine Action member on the run
articles.summary: Sean Middlebrough is convicted in his absence over a break-in at a British defence firm in Bristol.
articles.body:
A key member of Palestine Action, who is currently on the run, has been convicted in his absence over a break-in that caused damage put at £1.2m to an arms firm.

Sean Middlebrough, 33, originally from Liverpool, absconded in October last year after being granted bail for his brother's wedding. The self-proclaimed revolutionary communist has since sent messages to supporters describing himself as a "prisoner of war".

His trial began this summer in his absence and last month the jury convicted him of criminal damage by a majority of nine-to-one.

Prosecutors told the court Middlebrough had helped to plan and organise the August 2024 break-in at Elbit Systems in Bristol, a British defence firm with an Israeli parent company. The break-in happened 10 months before the government banned the group under counter-terrorism powers.

During the break-in, other members of Palestine Action rammed the van into Elbit's factory and, once inside, set about destroying as much equipment as they could find, including military drones that they believed would be used in Gaza.

The firm says that claim is untrue and that nothing produced at the Bristol facility goes to Israel.

Prosecutors told the court that Middlebrough's role included taking part in a planning meeting in Liverpool arranged with the help of encrypted communications.

He provided £890 to fund the the plot, including £600 that prosecutors said was used by another organiser to buy equipment used for the break-in.

That kit included sledgehammers, one of which was used by Samuel Corner to severely injure a police officer by fracturing her spine as she crouched on the ground.

Corner is now serving a seven year and eight month jail sentence for criminal damage and inflicting grievous bodily harm on Sgt Kate Evans.

The jury at Middlebrough's Old Bailey trial was not told why he was not in the dock along with the seven other alleged organisers.

While he was convicted in August of criminal damage, the trial of all eight defendants on other charges came to a halt when the jury failed to reach any other verdicts.

A retrial has been provisionally listed for June 2028. Seven of the eight face an allegation of criminal damage.

All but one of the defendants, including Middlebrough, face a further allegation of violent disorder. They deny all outstanding charges.

When Middlebrough was first charged over the incident, he was remanded into custody and he then began sending a podcast to supporters from jail, describing himself as a political prisoner.

The recordings were published on Spotify and later stopped by the prison authorities.

On 20 October last year a senior judge granted him temporary bail to go to his brother's wedding.

Middlebrough was permitted to first go to Liverpool and then briefly stay in West Yorkshire and was ordered to surrender to HMP Wandsworth in south London on 24 October.

He never showed up and a judge later issued a warrant for his arrest.

Police believe Middlebrough, known to friends as Shibby, was helped to leave the UK by a well-organised network of supporters.

Since his disappearance, he has sent messages to supporters, which have been published, saying he refuses to be "held as an Israeli prisoner of war in a British prison".

Reporting of Middlebrough's conviction was delayed because of a separate prosecution in which he and another man were accused of planning to carry out a Palestine Action-themed protest at Boris Johnson's 2022 wedding party.

Middlebrough's trial on that allegation has now been put back indefinitely for legal reasons.

Judge Patrick Field KC, the judge in Middlebrough's trial over the Elbit break-in, lifted the reporting restriction on his conviction at a hearing on Monday morning.

He is the fifth Palestine Action supporter to have been convicted over the attack.

Two more trials of alleged participants are expected.

BBC News has contacted the police for comment.

articles.title: Fashion and costume designer Bob Mackie, who made stars sparkle, dies at 87
articles.summary: The legendary fashion and costume designer Bob Mackie, who dressed divas from Cher to Diana Ross in glittering, eye-catching designs, has died at age 87, according to his social media accounts.
articles.body: The legendary fashion and costume designer Bob Mackie, who dressed divas from Cher to Diana Ross in glittering, eye-catching designs, has died at age 87, according to his social media accounts. “It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr. Bob Mackie passed away today. He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do,” read a post on his Instagram account. “His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world.” Over decades of designing for the A-list, Mackie’s name became synonymous with Hollywood glamour. Nicknamed the Sultan of Sequins, the Rajah of Rhinestones and the Guru of Glitter, Mackie’s designs — often amped up with jewels, crystals, feather and fringe — were the ultimate match for larger-than-life stars like Dolly Parton, Judy Garland and Tina Turner. The designer is best known for his longtime collaboration with Cher, whom he dressed on television and on tour. The designer first made a splash when he dressed the star for the 1974 Met Gala in a barely-there, sheer illusion dress, her arms and legs swathed in white feathers. “People were horrified,” he later recalled to Interview Magazine. “They thought, that’s not fashion, she’s just naked at the Metropolitan.” Nude illusion looks — often ornamented with glitter, feathers, and other Mackie motifs — became a staple look for the designer. His penchant for drawing attention paid off: Cher’s Met Gala look was featured in Vogue, then in Time. Cher spoke lovingly about the designer. “He is such an important person in my life,” the superstar said in 2024. “He helped me create a different me.” Mackie said his career grew out of a lifelong obsession with the glitz and glamour of show business. “I was never all that interested in fashion, as much as I was in costume design,” he told Vogue. “All through high school, I was all about putting on plays, that sort of thing.” Mackie became best-known for designs that blur the boundaries between fashion and costumes. The clothes became part of a client’s persona, one of the tools that helped transform an entertainer into an icon. “I could create characters for [them] that weren’t always specified in the script,” Mackie said. “When you’re designing for performers, you have to think about what does the audience want to see them look like — especially if they’re playing big theaters or stadiums.” Even in the early stages of his career, Mackie made waves. Working under his mentor Jean Louis, he sketched the original design for the bedazzled, body-clinging gown Marilyn Monroe wore in 1962 for President John F. Kennedy‘s birthday celebration in New York. Mackie’s flair for the ostentatious sometimes flirted with comedy, a sensibility he honed while serving as the costume designer for “The Carol Burnett Show.” He said he was careful to walk a fine line and avoid going “too far.” “You want it to be more clever than that,” he told Interview, citing as an example the “curtain rod dress” in which he styled Burnett for a parody of “Gone with the Wind,” one of the show’s most famous sight gags. Burnett estimated that Mackie created 17,000 costumes for her show’s 11-year run. “There are fashion designers, but they can’t do costumes,” she said. “And then there are costume designers that don’t do fashion. But Bob does it all. He’s the whole ball of wax.” Sometimes the comedy was more overt. Mackie dressed Elton John, for instance, in an absurd Donald Duck costume for a 1980 concert in New York City’s Central Park. “I was dancing across the stage, falling over myself, and I just couldn’t sing for laughing,” John recalled in “Who Is Mackie?,” a short film. “Because it looked ridiculous, but it looked fabulous.” Mackie’s popularity continued into the modern day, with his archive coveted by a new generation of stars. Sabrina Carpenter and Zendaya have sported Mackie looks on the red carpet. Miley Cyrus wore an archival Mackie dress, covered in strings of crystals, to perform at the 2024 Grammys. The dress was classic Mackie: Designed for a performer and moving with Cyrus as she danced, without overpowering or upstaging her. Mackie said he was happy to see younger stars excited about his work. Today, “the performers are younger and braver and they’ve watched a lot of the old stuff,” he told Interview. “That’s how all these young Disney girls, these famous girls who’ve been wearing some of my old clothes discover me.” For his stage and screen work, Mackie won nine Emmys, induction into the Television Academy Hall of Fame and three Academy Award nominations. In 1999, he received a retrospective at the Museum at FIT. More recently, he won a Tony Award for the musical “The Cher Show” and a lifetime achievement award from the Council of Fashion Designers of America. Mackie was even tapped by Mattel to produce a line of outfits for Barbie dolls. He helped diversify the doll’s looks, crafting Barbies in the mold of some of his most famous designs and veering away from the homogenous blonde Barbies of the past. Mackie’s rendition was “more fantasy-oriented,” he said. “She could be anything we wanted her to be.” Fern Mallis, former executive director of CFDA and founder of New York Fashion Week, credited him with many of the red carpet trends we see today. “When he did fashion shows, they were so spectacular and theatrical,” she told CNN in 2019. “He invented the naked dresses with the strategically placed beads. Now everyone who walks the red carpet, or designs for the red carpet, owes him a debt of gratitude, whether they know it or not. He’s a treasure; he’s one of a kind.”

articles.title: How Israel systematically dismantles Palestinian life in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: B’Tselem says settlement expansion, displacement and curbs are not isolated abuses, but decades-old, coordinated system.
articles.body:
Bethlehem, occupied West Bank – On any given week, Palestinians across the occupied West Bank can experience dozens of what appear to be isolated acts of Israeli violence and suppression.

In early September, Israeli forces killed two teenagers during a military raid in al-Mughayyir, east of Ramallah. Days later in Masafer Yatta, Israeli forces demolished every home in Khirbet al-Tabban, leaving about 70 people, including 30 children, without shelter. In Qusra, south of Nablus, settlers have kept three families under siege inside their homes for more than a month, cutting off their water and power.

In a new report published on Monday, Israeli rights group B’Tselem argued these are not separate incidents. Together, they work towards a single end: Making Palestinian life on the land unsustainable and replacing it with permanent Israeli control. The reality in the West Bank, the group said, is “neither a temporary crisis nor a collection of random human rights violations”.

Instead, it is “an accelerated and explicit phase in an ongoing project of elimination that operates within the Israeli apartheid regime and is driven by a settler-colonial logic of dispossession, displacement, and the establishment of Jewish-Israeli sovereignty”, the publication – called The Elimination Project – added.

Drawing on nearly 2,000 Palestinian testimonies, the report said that seemingly separate Israeli violations are part of what it called “a comprehensive mechanism of elimination”.

By “elimination”, B’Tselem referred to the systematic dismantling of Palestinian society, eroding its institutions, economy, freedom of movement and social life.

The report placed this within what it called the “basic logic of settler colonialism”: Establishing “permanent settler sovereignty over a territory already inhabited by an Indigenous people” by “pushing them out, dispossessing them and dismantling their collective existence”.

It identifies five interconnected fronts through which that process operates: Violence and intimidation, movement restrictions, economic strangulation, social and political destruction, and ethnic cleansing and territorial takeover.

B’Tselem traced that logic to the 2017 “Decisive Plan” authored by Bezalel Smotrich, now Israel’s finance minister. The plan, the group said, gave Palestinians three choices: Accept Jewish supremacy while giving up their national claims, leave, or face violent suppression.

None of this is new, the report argued; the mechanism has run for decades. What has changed is that it has grown far more severe and open, escalating since the current far-right government took office in late 2022 and sharply after the start of the genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

For roughly 3.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem, that system is felt in the steady narrowing of daily life: Roads they cannot use, land they cannot reach, and fewer places where they can safely live, work and move.

By December 2025, Israel had at least 925 physical obstacles set up across the West Bank, the most the United Nations has recorded in two decades.

Yusef Kashur, a driver and father of six from Dura, south of Hebron, told B’Tselem that the growing network of gates and checkpoints had turned his work into a “torment”, forcing him onto long, dangerous backroads and to turn down fares he once relied on.

“These drives are exhausting, take a very long time, and the fuel costs so much that I don’t make enough to cover our household needs,” he said.

The restrictions feed a wider collapse. Under an occupation that controls its borders, trade and revenue, the West Bank economy has little room of its own, and it has buckled: Unemployment at the end of last year had roughly doubled to 27.5 percent compared to October 2023, driven in part by the freezing of work permits for about 115,000 Palestinians .

The squeeze is deliberate, the report argued: A family that cannot earn is easier to uproot, and when Palestinians fall back on their own land, the pressure follows them there.

After losing his job inside Israel, Jamil Abu Rayan turned to his grapevines near Halhul, only to find settlers had established an illegal outpost at his main plot. Soldiers also barred him from another plot, calling it “[Israeli] state land”.

He told B’Tselem he lost about 60 percent of his 2025 grape harvest and that he can no longer properly work his land.

Recounting a late January attack in the South Hebron Hills , where entire communities face forcible displacement, Isma’il Khalayleh told the rights group earlier this year that a settler pressed a rifle to his forehead and gave him a deadline: “I’m giving you 24 hours to leave this place.”

Agricultural and grazing outposts have “violently taken control” of nearly 20 percent of the West Bank, according to Israeli settlement-watchdog group Peace Now. More than 1,600 settler attacks were recorded by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) last year.

The same pressure extends to where Palestinians can build; Israeli authorities make it “virtually impossible for Palestinians to obtain building permits”, according to OCHA, leaving many families who build without them under constant threat of Israeli demolition.

As Palestinian communities are cleared, more illegal Israeli settlements expand. The current government has approved a record 104 new settlements since 2022.

The suppression also extends to the institutions that hold Palestinian society together, with B’Tselem documenting a series of raids and closure orders faced by charities, trade unions and universities.

Ahmad Dweikat told the rights group that in May 2026, soldiers ransacked a Nablus association he co-founded to help women, children and families, confiscating computers and cash, including money set aside for orphans.

Running beneath all of it is the military’s lethal force. B’Tselem counted about 1,087 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces in the West Bank since October 2023, roughly a quarter of them children.

Among them was Jamil Hanani, a 17-year-old boy from Beit Furik who was shot during an army raid on the town. “It’s as if they go out hunting, only they’re hunting human beings,” his father, ‘Atef Hanani, told B’Tselem.

For years, foreign governments have urged Israel to show restraint. That framing misses the point, B’Tselem argued: The violence, closures and demolitions are not failures of the system, but the system working as intended.

Sanctioning an individual settler, reopening a road or freezing a single settlement plan would “leave intact the structure that produces violence, dispossession, and oppression”, it said.

Seen this way, the question is not whether each individual act is an isolated violation, but what they produce together: A steadily shrinking space for Palestinians to live, work, build and remain on their land.

And the West Bank, the report argued, cannot be read apart from Gaza. The two are “different manifestations of the same regime project, directed against Palestinians’ ability to exist as a people”.

articles.title: Strictly's Horwood revels in role as villain in Bristol panto
articles.summary: The Strictly Come Dancing judge is sharing the stage with Andy Ford and BBC Bristol's Joe Sims.
articles.body:
The line-up for one of a city's biggest Christmas pantomimes has been announced.

Craig Revel Horwood, Andy Ford and BBC Radio Bristol's Joe Sims are all joining the cast for a rendition of Sleeping Beauty at the Bristol Hippodrome for the month of December.

Strictly Come Dancing judge Revel Horwood has been cast as this year's pantomime villain, Sleeping Beauty's wicked aunt Carabosse and is relishing the prospect.

"She's a wicked fairy, which is totally unlike me darling," said Revel Horwood.

Main Post Office branch to close in November

'Saying no to sex once should have been enough'

Defibrillator installed after fatal cardiac arrest

Revel Horwood has a reputation for being the pantomime villain for the critiques and feedback he offers to some of Strictly's contestants and says that image has eased the transition from ballroom judge to fantasy evil aunt.

"The beauty of panto is that I can play both parts, I can break the fourth wall and be Craig Revel Horwood as well as Carabosse.

"It's great because you can go into the whole thing of being a villain and it's way more outrageous than when I'm on Strictly.

"On Strictly I'm there judging and it's the audience that have branded me the villain, but I'm just telling people the truth darling.

"[Whereas] playing the villains in panto, it's totally dishonest, it's totally fantastic and I love it because it's makeup, it's costumes and it's over the top."

Revel Horwood says he "absolutely loves" Bristol but admits he is having trouble understanding the accent of his onstage right hand man, The Henchman, played by Broadchurch and Doctor Who actor Joe Sims.

Sims, who also hosts BBC Radio Bristol's breakfast programme has promised to help him get to grips with the lingo and says the opportunity is a Bristolian's dream come true.

"When someone gave me the opportunity to be Craig Revel Horwood's right hand man, I was just thinking it sounds absolutely amazing," said Sims.

"The idea that this year my kids are going to be there... it feels like a bucket list thing."

Sleeping Beauty debuts at the Bristol Hippodrome on 4 December and closes on 4 January.
